text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
- Opposition SPD says federal budget deficit already exceeded 60 billion mark threshold for 1996 in August, reaching 63 billion marks some four months before the end of the year.
- German parliament again debates government decision earlier this month to cut workers' sick pay to 80 percent from 100 percent.
- Kohl concerned about latest developments in Middle East, once again urges Netanyahu to push peace process forward
- German government wants sick pay cut for all workers, unions and employers urged to sign new contracts

- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, in New York, warns counterpart Warren Christopher against overplaying its role as the world's only world power. Says "unilateralism" could be counterproductive for Washington
- Bonn mayor fears loss of jobs if Bundesrat, or upper house of parliament, votes as expected on Friday to move to Berlin later this decade along with government and lower house

- IG Metall braces for strikes as dispute over full sick pay escalates in Bavaria. Bavarian union leaders plan to cancel existing wage contract at the end of January 1997 in order to free its hand for possible strikes
- Members of CDU urge new capital gains tax on profits from share price gains and property value increases
- DAX index reaches second straight record high, boosted by rate cut in Switzerland as well as weaker mark
- Tense tax debate breaks out in the CDU, several stakes call for "more fairness" and heavier tax burdens on capital gains and lower taxes on wages
- Bundesrat to vote on moving to Berlin with government and lower house
- Berlin cigarette gang broken up by police after three leaders of murderous gang arrested
